item.title: Global sensitivity analysis
item.description:
The situation this solves

You have a model. It has parameters. You do not know most of them exactly — you know roughly what each one could be, because somebody measured it once in a different system, or estimated it from a figure, or nobody has ever measured it at all.

So your prediction is not a number. It is a spread. Run the model across everything you might plausibly believe and the answers come out wildly different.

The question worth asking is not “what does the model predict?” It is:

Which of the numbers I don’t know is responsible for the answers coming out so differently?

That is all global sensitivity analysis is. Answer it and you know exactly which measurement would be worth making — which is the most useful thing a model can tell you before the fieldwork is done.

The worked example throughout is a winter tick–moose model with 13 uncertain parameters, analysed over 50 years.

Step 0. Why not just change one parameter at a time?

The instinct is to take your baseline parameter set, nudge one parameter by 10%, see how much the answer moves, and repeat. This is local sensitivity, also called OAT (one-at-a-time). Three things go wrong with it.

It only describes one point

The derivative at your baseline tells you nothing about behaviour anywhere else. Our model has an attachment probability that saturates at 1. Near saturation the local sensitivity to the attachment rate is exactly zero — every tick already finds a host, so making them better at finding hosts changes nothing.

Across its full plausible range, is the single most important parameter in the model.

A local analysis run from a host-rich baseline would have reported “attachment doesn’t matter” and been completely wrong. Drag the baseline below to watch this happen:

viewof lbeta0 = Inputs.range([-7.3, -4.7], {value: -5.0, step: 0.05,
  label: "Baseline log₁₀ β"})
viewof hosts = Inputs.range([500, 6000], {value: 3000, step: 100,
  label: "Host abundance"})
// Schematic saturating attachment: P = 1 - exp(-beta * H * tau)
attach = (lb) => 1 - Math.exp(-Math.pow(10, lb) * hosts * 165)
satCurve = {
  const out = [];
  for (let lb = -7.3; lb <= -4.7; lb += 0.02) out.push({lb: lb, P: attach(lb)});
  return out;
}
// Local slope at the baseline, drawn as a short tangent segment
tangent = {
  const h = 0.02;
  const slope = (attach(lbeta0 + h) - attach(lbeta0 - h)) / (2 * h);
  const y0 = attach(lbeta0);
  return {
    slope: slope,
    seg: [{lb: lbeta0 - 0.5, P: y0 - 0.5 * slope},
          {lb: lbeta0 + 0.5, P: y0 + 0.5 * slope}]
  };
}
Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 720),
  height: 340,
  marginLeft: 60,
  marginBottom: 45,
  style: {fontSize: "13px", background: "transparent"},
  x: {label: "log₁₀ attachment rate β →", grid: true, domain: [-7.3, -4.7]},
  y: {label: "↑ Attachment probability", grid: true, domain: [-0.05, 1.05]},
  marks: [
    Plot.areaY(satCurve, {x: "lb", y: "P", fill: "#2c6e63", fillOpacity: 0.08}),
    Plot.line(satCurve, {x: "lb", y: "P", stroke: "#2c6e63", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.line(tangent.seg, {x: "lb", y: "P", stroke: "#c0563f",
      strokeWidth: 2.5, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.dot([{lb: lbeta0, P: attach(lbeta0)}], {x: "lb", y: "P",
      fill: "#c0563f", r: 5}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#999"})
  ]
})
html`<p style="margin:0.6rem 0 0 0; font-size:0.95rem;">
Local slope at this baseline: <b>${tangent.slope.toFixed(3)}</b> per decade of β.
Full range of the output across all plausible β: <b>${
  (Math.max(...satCurve.map(d => d.P)) - Math.min(...satCurve.map(d => d.P))).toFixed(3)
}</b>.
${tangent.slope < 0.02
  ? "<span style='color:#c0563f'><b>The local analysis says β is irrelevant. It is not.</b></span>"
  : "Here the baseline sits on the steep part, so local and global happen to agree."}
</p>`

It cannot see interactions

Holding everything else fixed means you never observe that behaves differently depending on the aggregation parameter . In our run the total indices sum to about 2.4, against 1.0 for a purely additive model — so most of what the model is doing is interaction. OAT would have missed nearly all of it.

It explores almost nothing

With 13 parameters, moving along 13 axes out from a single point covers a vanishingly small fraction of a 13-dimensional box.

Global sensitivity analysis instead varies all parameters simultaneously across their full plausible ranges, and asks: of all the variation we see in the output, how much is attributable to each input?

Step 1. Understand what the answer will look like

Before any machinery, it is worth understanding what a variance decomposition actually claims. It is simpler than the notation suggests, and you can see the whole idea in four model runs.

Two parameters, each set Low or High. Four runs, four answers. Drag the answers and watch the split change:

viewof LL = Inputs.range([0, 20], {value: 1, step: 0.5, label: "β low, μ low"})
viewof HL = Inputs.range([0, 20], {value: 9, step: 0.5, label: "β high, μ low"})
viewof LH = Inputs.range([0, 20], {value: 2, step: 0.5, label: "β low, μ high"})
viewof HH = Inputs.range([0, 20], {value: 18, step: 0.5, label: "β high, μ high"})
sob = {
  const y = [LL, HL, LH, HH];
  const m = (LL + HL + LH + HH) / 4;
  const V = y.reduce((s, v) => s + (v - m) ** 2, 0) / 4;
  const bL = (LL + LH) / 2, bH = (HL + HH) / 2;
  const uL = (LL + HL) / 2, uH = (LH + HH) / 2;
  const Vb = ((bL - m) ** 2 + (bH - m) ** 2) / 2;
  const Vu = ((uL - m) ** 2 + (uH - m) ** 2) / 2;
  const Vs = Math.max(0, V - Vb - Vu);
  return {
    V: V, bL: bL, bH: bH, uL: uL, uH: uH,
    beta:   V > 0 ? Vb / V : 0,
    mu:     V > 0 ? Vu / V : 0,
    shared: V > 0 ? Vs / V : 0,
    effLo: HL - LL,
    effHi: HH - LH
  };
}
Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 720),
  height: 150,
  marginLeft: 70,
  marginTop: 30,
  marginBottom: 50,
  style: {fontSize: "13px", background: "transparent"},
  x: {label: "Share of the spread →", domain: [0, 1], grid: true,
      tickFormat: d => Math.round(d * 100) + "%"},
  y: {label: null},
  color: {
    domain: ["β alone", "μ alone", "shared"],
    range: ["#2c6e63", "#7a9e6b", "#b9b4a8"],
    legend: true
  },
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(
      [{p: "β alone", v: sob.beta}, {p: "μ alone", v: sob.mu},
       {p: "shared", v: sob.shared}],
      {x: "v", fill: "p", y: () => "", sort: null}
    ),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})
html`<p style="margin:0.4rem 0 0.9rem 0; font-size:0.95rem;">${
  sob.V === 0
    ? "All four answers are the same, so there is no spread to divide."
    : Math.abs(sob.effHi - sob.effLo) < 0.5
      ? `β lifts the answer by <b>${sob.effLo}</b> whether μ is low or high. Its
         effect does not depend on μ, so <b>the shared piece is zero</b> and the
         two totals add to exactly 1.`
      : `β lifts the answer by <b>${sob.effLo}</b> when μ is low, but by
         <b>${sob.effHi}</b> when μ is high. That inconsistency is the shared
         piece — it belongs to neither parameter on its own.`
}</p>`
Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 720),
  height: 190,
  marginLeft: 70,
  marginTop: 30,
  marginBottom: 50,
  style: {fontSize: "13px", background: "transparent"},
  x: {label: "Total index →", grid: true},
  y: {label: null},
  color: {
    domain: ["on its own", "via interaction"],
    range: ["#2c6e63", "#d6d2c6"],
    legend: true
  },
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(
      [{p: "β", part: "on its own", v: sob.beta},
       {p: "β", part: "via interaction", v: sob.shared},
       {p: "μ", part: "on its own", v: sob.mu},
       {p: "μ", part: "via interaction", v: sob.shared}],
      {x: "v", y: "p", fill: "part", sort: null}
    ),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})
html`<p style="margin:0.4rem 0 0 0; font-size:0.95rem;">
Totals add to <b>${(sob.beta + sob.mu + 2 * sob.shared).toFixed(3)}</b>.
${sob.shared > 0.005
  ? "They exceed 1 because the shared piece is counted in both parameters' totals — it genuinely belongs to both."
  : "With no interaction, they add to exactly 1."}
</p>`

At the default values the arithmetic is:

answer
L L 1
H L 9
L H 2
H H 18

Total spread (variance) = 46.25.

’s own piece. Average when is low = 1.5, when high = 13.5. Far apart, so ’s piece is 36.0 — that is 77.8% of the spread.

’s own piece. Average when low = 5.0, when high = 10.0. Closer, so ’s piece is 6.25 — 13.5%.

Left over: 4.0, or 8.6%. This is the shared piece, and here is why it exists: lifts the answer by 8 when is low, but by 16 when is high. ’s effect depends on . That inconsistency cannot be credited to either one alone, so it gets a piece of its own.

Exactly. Nothing lost, nothing double counted. There is only one way to do this split and it always adds up — that exactness is the point.

The one sentence to remember

How much the average answer moves when you learn a parameter’s value is that parameter’s piece of the spread. We cannot rerun history with held fixed, so instead we compare the average over every run where was low against the average over every run where it was high.

Step 2. The formal version

That four-run split generalises. For a model with independent inputs, the output variance decomposes uniquely:

  • — variance explained by on its own
  • — the extra variance from and acting together, beyond their separate effects
  • and so on for higher orders.

Divide through by and every term becomes a share summing to 1. This is the Sobol decomposition — three plain words wearing a disguise. Variance is just how spread out the answers are. Decomposition is cutting that spread into pieces. Sobol is a person’s name (Ilya Sobol, who worked it out) and carries no meaning at all.

The two indices you report

First-order index

The share of variance explained by alone. Equivalently: the fraction of uncertainty you would eliminate by learning exactly.

Total index

alone plus everything it does through interactions. Equivalently: the uncertainty that would remain if you learned every parameter except .

Three diagnostics fall straight out:

Reading Meaning
how much of this parameter’s influence runs through interactions
model is additive; parameters act independently
strong interactions; the same variance is attributed to several parameters because it belongs to none of them alone
genuinely negligible — safe to fix and drop from the analysis

Variance is the right currency because it is model-free: no assumption of linearity, monotonicity or additivity. Compare a correlation coefficient, which only sees monotonic trends. In our run showed a large Sobol index but a near-zero Spearman correlation, because its effect is hump-shaped. A correlation-based method would have declared it unimportant.

Step 3. Choose the parameter ranges

This is the step with the least mathematics and by far the most consequence.

Every index is conditional on the ranges. A parameter given a wide range will tend to look important; the same parameter pinned to a narrow range will look irrelevant. This is not a flaw — it is correct behaviour, because the question being asked is “given what we don’t know, what drives the uncertainty in our prediction?” A parameter you know precisely should rank low, even if the model is mechanistically very sensitive to it.

What that meant in our case:

  • log10_beta_M spans three decades because nobody has ever measured it. It came out top. That ranking is a statement about our ignorance, not purely about the biology.
  • lambda spans ±40% because Drew & Samuel counted eggs directly. It ranked low partly because we know it well.
  • mu_E’s two endpoints are the two competing readings of the same paper, so its index measures what the unresolved argument costs us.
Always report the ranges next to the indices

An index without its range is not interpretable. A parameter can score low for three completely different reasons — we know it well, it genuinely does nothing, or it cannot do anything however wide the range. Those are three different findings. Say which one you mean.

Three practical rules that made the ranges defensible:

Set ranges on the interpretable quantity, then invert. We set the virulence by asking “how many ticks kill half a moose?” and solving

Nobody can eyeball whether is sensible. Everybody can judge 38,000 ticks.

Sample on a log scale when a range spans decades, otherwise 90% of your draws land in the top decade.

Make ranges track the model’s structure. Our beta_for() helper derives ’s range from the current host numbers, because what matters is , never alone.

Where nothing is measured at all, bound it by something you do know. Winter tick is established in Yukon, so ; it is at its northern range edge, so is not enormous. We set ’s range to the values putting between roughly 1 and 70. Indirect, but a real constraint and far better than three arbitrary decades.

rng_dyn2 <- list(
  # beta_M: never measured. Bounded so R0 runs from ~1 to ~67.
  log10_beta_M  = c(-7.3, -4.7),

  # mu_E: egg + free-living larval mortality, from egg-to-questing
  # survival of 30% down to 2%:  mu_E = -log(survival) / tau_E
  mu_E          = c(0.01003, 0.03260),

  # mu_N: attached nymph mortality, nymph-to-adult survival 50% to 10%
  mu_N          = c(0.00420, 0.01396),

  lambda        = c(1500, 5000),      # eggs per surviving female

  # Stage durations: the climate levers. Arthropod development runs
  # 2-3x faster per 10 C, and Yukon is projected 4-6 C warmer.
  tau_E         = c(75, 180),
  tau_Q         = c(30, 120),
  tau_A         = c(140, 200),

  M0            = c(500, 6000),       # host abundance
  U0            = c(100, 6000),

  # alpha_M: set as the burden that kills half a moose, then inverted
  #   150,000 ticks -> log10 = -7.29  (tolerant)
  #     5,000 ticks -> log10 = -5.81  (vulnerable)
  log10_alpha_M = c(-7.29, -5.81),

  k             = c(0.02, 1.00),      # aggregation; small = more clumped
  rho_M         = c(1.00, 1.20),      # moose finite rate of increase
  rho_U         = c(1.00, 1.35)
)

Step 4. Choose the design

You need parameter sets that cover the space efficiently. The options, with cost for parameters:

Design Cost Analysis it supports
Full factorial, levels ANOVA
Fractional factorial ANOVA
eFAST (fast99) Fourier decomposition
Sobol Monte Carlo Sobol estimators
Morris screening only — ranks, no quantities
Latin hypercube PRCC, regression — not ANOVA

We used eFAST, for three reasons:

  1. A full factorial at 3 levels samples each parameter at only three points. Our output spans about 10 orders of magnitude, and three points cannot describe a surface that curved. The curvature you miss gets misattributed as “interaction”.
  2. eFAST samples continuously along space-filling curves, so it handles nonlinearity properly.
  3. Cost is linear in the number of parameters. Going from 7 to 13 parameters cost us 2,100 → 3,900 runs instead of 2,187 → 1.6 million.

How eFAST samples

Every parameter gets its own frequency, and the design walks a single curve through parameter space. As a scalar advances, each parameter oscillates:

where is parameter ’s distinct frequency and is the transform making uniform over its range.

That sounds like a strange thing to do. Here is the trick: because each parameter wiggles at a different rate, the model’s answer wiggles back at that same rate. Take the Fourier spectrum of the output, and the power sitting at parameter ’s frequency is . It is the same idea as picking one instrument out of a recording because you know its pitch. No fitting, no guessing.

Why LHS does not work with ANOVA

multisensi’s default engine is ANOVA, which needs each factor to take a few repeated levels so there are residual degrees of freedom. A continuous Latin hypercube gives every factor distinct values, the model is saturated, and the decomposition fails. LHS is a perfectly good design — but pair it with PRCC or regression, not ANOVA.

Step 5. Run the model

run_design(X, years = 50, out_var = "M")

takes the design table and returns:

IN   3900 rows (parameter sets)  x  13 columns (parameters)
OUT  3900 rows (parameter sets)  x  51 columns (years)

Row out is the trajectory produced by row in. Note the output is multivariate — 51 numbers per run, not one. That is what the next step is for.

Analyse the log when the process is multiplicative

Our tick population is multiplicative — each year is last year times a growth factor — so over 50 years small parameter differences compound into orders of magnitude. On a raw scale the variance is then owned by the handful of runs that exploded, no single parameter explains the level (because the level is a product of all of them), first-order indices collapse to nearly zero, and everything piles into interaction.

Taking logs turns that product into a sum, which is exactly the additive structure a variance decomposition is built for, and the main effects reappear. Host populations vary far less, so they don’t need it.

Step 6. Reduce the output with PCA

We have 51 outputs, one per year. We could run 51 separate sensitivity analyses and get 51 sets of indices. Two reasons not to:

  1. It is unreadable. 13 parameters × 51 years × 2 index types = 1,326 numbers. There is no ranking in there a person can act on.
  2. The outputs are massively redundant. Year 30 and year 31 are almost the same number. Naively averaging 51 sets of indices would count the same information dozens of times over.

PCA finds a small set of orthogonal shapes that trajectories vary along. Instead of 51 correlated numbers per run, each run is described by a handful of uncorrelated component scores. In our run:

Component Variance explained What it represents
PC1 75.4% the overall level — how high or low the herd sits
PC2 14.2% the transient shape — early crash and partial recovery
PC3 3.8% early oscillation
PC4 2.6% negligible

Three components carry 93.4% of everything that varies between trajectories.

Why orthogonality is the whole point

This is the part usually glossed over, and it is the reason the PCA is there at all. PCA components are uncorrelated by construction, which means the total variance splits additively across them:

Because there is no overlap between components, you may analyse each one separately and then combine the results by a weighted sum without double counting. If the components were correlated — as the 51 yearly outputs are — that combination step would be invalid.

So the PCA is not cosmetic dimension reduction. It is what makes Step 8 mathematically legitimate.

There is an interpretation bonus too. Each component has a temporal loading profile showing how it weights each year, so you are no longer decomposing variance “at year 37” — you are decomposing variance in trajectory shape. Asking which parameters drive the overall level, and which drive the transient, is a better question than asking about any single year.

Step 7. Decompose the variance

Each component’s scores are one number per run, so this is now an ordinary scalar problem. eFAST estimates the decomposition from the Fourier spectrum:

Index How it is read off the spectrum Plain English
power at and its harmonics learn this one number and this much guesswork goes away
: everything except the other parameters’ frequencies learn all the others but not this one, and this much guesswork is left

Because it reads variance off a spectrum rather than fitting a model, there is no residual term. Nothing is left over.

Step 8. Aggregate to one number per parameter

Steps 6 and 7 give indices per component. To get one number per parameter, use the Generalised Sensitivity Index (Lamboni et al.) — the inertia-weighted average:

where is the index of parameter on component and is that component’s eigenvalue. Components are weighted by how much trajectory variation they actually explain, so PC1 at 75.4% dominates and PC3 at 3.8% barely contributes.

This weighted sum is only valid because the components are orthogonal. That is the payoff from Step 6. Averaging the 51 raw yearly indices instead would count the same information dozens of times over.

The whole thing in R

library(multisensi)

gsa_time <- multisensi(
  design        = fast99,               # 1. how the sample is built
  model         = run_design,           # 2. run the model on every row
  reduction     = basis.ACP,            # 3. PCA the 51 yearly outputs
  scale         = FALSE,                #    covariance, not correlation
  design.args   = list(
    factors = names(parameters_range),
    n       = 1000,                     # runs per parameter
    q       = "qunif",
    q.arg   = lapply(parameters_range,
                     function(r) list(min = r[1], max = r[2]))
  ),
  analysis      = analysis.sensitivity, # 4. decompose the variance
  analysis.args = list(keep.outputs = FALSE)
)

summary(gsa_time)

What comes back:

Object Contents
gsa$L loadings — the shape over time of each component, length 51
gsa$H scores — one per run, how strongly that run shows the shape
gsa$lambda eigenvalues, the variance of each component
gsa$mSI first-order indices
gsa$tSI total indices

scale = FALSE means PCA on the covariance, not the correlation matrix. That is correct here because all 51 columns are the same quantity in the same units — standardising would give a quiet year the same weight as a year of collapse.

design = fast99 means this is not ANOVA

design = fast99 with analysis = analysis.sensitivity is the eFAST route. ANOVA (analysis.anoasg) is the other engine, used when you pass discrete levels through design.args instead of ranges. They estimate the same quantity by different means — see the comparison at the end.

Reading the results

Our run, watching the moose herd:

Parameter (alone) (total) via interactions
log10_beta_M 0.31 0.80 61%
mu_E 0.10 0.42 76%
k 0.26 0.41 37%
rho_M 0.03 0.27 89%
lambda 0.01 0.17 94%
log10_alpha_M 0.005 0.16 97%
rho_U 0.03 0.16 81%

Totals sum to about 2.4, not 1. The model is strongly non-additive. The practical consequence is blunt: “increasing X does Y to moose” is not a sentence this model supports without stating what the other parameters are doing. Any single-parameter policy claim needs a caveat.

A big gap between and means context-dependent. log10_alpha_M has a first-order index of 0.005 and a total of 0.16 — on its own it does essentially nothing, but it matters in combination. Virulence only bites once attachment has already put enough ticks on the animal.

A small gap means the parameter acts independently. k at 0.26 / 0.41 has the most autonomous effect in the model.

Indices are unsigned. They tell you how much, never which way. Direction has to come from somewhere else — a scatter of output against each parameter, or PRCC on a random or LHS sample. This matters: rho_U turned out negative (more alternative hosts → fewer moose), which no sensitivity index would have told us.

What to do with the answer

  1. Measure the top-ranked uncertain parameter. beta_M at 0.80 total, with no empirical basis at all. That is the highest-value fieldwork in the system.
  2. Settle cheap disputes. mu_E at 0.42 comes down to one sentence in a 1986 paper.
  3. Fix and forget the negligible ones. Anything with can be pinned at its baseline in future work.
  4. Report ranges alongside indices. Always.

Pitfalls

Indices are conditional on the ranges. beta_M was allowed three decades; rho_M was allowed 12%. Some of beta’s dominance is that, and you must say so.

eFAST assumes independent inputs. We have a live violation: mu_E and mu_N are the same disputed reading of the same paper. If one value is right, the other almost certainly is too — so the sweep explores combinations that cannot both be true, while the indices are computed as though the two are independent. State this in the methods rather than hoping nobody notices.

eFAST cannot warn you when it fails. It has no residual by construction. If is too small or frequencies interfere, you get plausible-looking numbers with no signal that anything went wrong. ANOVA’s residual is a feature — a built-in confession that “27% of this I could not explain”.

The trade-off runs opposite to intuition:

eFAST ANOVA
Functional form agnostic limited by grid and formula order
Cost
Warns you when it fails no yes — the residual

Both engines estimate the same Sobol decomposition. They differ in the estimator, not the target. Which is the argument for running both on a small subset once and checking they agree:

top6 <- c("log10_beta_M", "mu_E", "k", "rho_M", "lambda", "log10_alpha_M")
a <- run_gsa_dyn(as_levels(rng_dyn2[top6]))   # ANOVA, has a residual
b <- run_gsa_dyn(rng_dyn2[top6])              # eFAST, does not
plot_gsi(a); plot_gsi(b)                      # same ranking?

Watch for near-zero variance. Indices summing above 1 in the early years of our run were exactly this: tiny variance plus a finite sample gives noisy estimates.

Different questions need different analyses. cannot rank alpha_M, k, rho_M or rho_U — they do not appear in it, because is a low-density quantity. Establishment and host collapse are different questions.

Further reading

  • Saltelli, A. et al. (2008). Global Sensitivity Analysis: The Primer. The standard reference.
  • Lamboni, M., Monod, H. & Makowski, D. (2011). Multivariate sensitivity analysis to measure global contribution of input factors in dynamic models. Reliability Engineering & System Safety. The GSI.
  • Marino, S. et al. (2008). A methodology for performing global uncertainty and sensitivity analysis in systems biology. Journal of Theoretical Biology. The LHS/PRCC route, widely used in epidemiology.
  • The multisensi, sensitivity and sensobol R packages.

The winter tick model behind this page was built at the PIMS summer school on Mathematics of Multiscale Interactions, 2026.

item.title: Logistic growth
item.description:
The problem with exponential growth

The simplest population model says each individual contributes offspring at a constant per-capita rate :

which gives . This is a fine description of a population that has just arrived somewhere empty, and a terrible description of one that has been there a while — it predicts unbounded growth forever.

The fix is to let the per-capita growth rate decline as the population fills up. The logistic model makes that decline linear:

Read the right-hand side as the correction term it is. When , the bracket is close to 1 and growth is nearly exponential. When , the bracket is zero and growth stops. When , the bracket is negative and the population declines. The parameter — the carrying capacity — is the density at which births exactly balance deaths.

Rearranged, this is the form you’ll usually see:

Play with it

The logistic equation has a closed-form solution, which is unusual and convenient:

Move the sliders and watch what each parameter actually controls.

viewof r = Inputs.range([0.05, 1.5], {value: 0.4, step: 0.05, label: "Intrinsic growth rate r"})
viewof K = Inputs.range([20, 400], {value: 200, step: 10, label: "Carrying capacity K"})
viewof N0 = Inputs.range([1, 400], {value: 10, step: 1, label: "Initial population N₀"})
traj = {
  const out = [];
  for (let t = 0; t <= 40; t += 0.2) {
    const N = K / (1 + ((K - N0) / N0) * Math.exp(-r * t));
    out.push({t: t, N: N});
  }
  return out;
}
Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 720),
  height: 380,
  marginLeft: 60,
  marginBottom: 45,
  style: {fontSize: "13px", background: "transparent"},
  x: {label: "Time →", grid: true},
  y: {label: "↑ Population N(t)", grid: true,
      domain: [0, Math.max(K, N0) * 1.15]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([K], {stroke: "#c0563f", strokeDasharray: "5,4"}),
    Plot.text([{t: 39, N: K}], {x: "t", y: "N", text: ["K"],
      dy: -10, fill: "#c0563f", fontWeight: "bold"}),
    Plot.line(traj, {x: "t", y: "N", stroke: "#2c6e63", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#999"})
  ]
})

In R

Solving it numerically is overkill given the closed form, but the numerical setup generalises to models that have no analytical solution, so it’s worth having:

library(deSolve)
library(ggplot2)

logistic <- function(t, state, parms) {
  with(as.list(c(state, parms)), {
    dN <- r * N * (1 - N / K)
    list(dN)
  })
}

out <- ode(
  y     = c(N = 10),
  times = seq(0, 40, by = 0.1),
  func  = logistic,
  parms = c(r = 0.4, K = 200)
) |> as.data.frame()

ggplot(out, aes(times, N)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 200, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#c0563f") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#2c6e63") +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Population size N(t)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

Assumptions worth remembering

The logistic model earns its simplicity by assuming a great deal:

  • Density dependence is linear. Real per-capita growth rates often decline non-linearly, and the theta-logistic model exists precisely to relax this.
  • No time lags. Individuals respond to current density instantly. Adding a delay to the density term is enough to generate oscillations.
  • No age or stage structure. Everyone reproduces identically, regardless of age or size.
  • No stochasticity. Both environmental variation and demographic noise are absent, which matters enormously at small .
  • Closed population. No immigration or emigration.
  • Constant environment. and don’t vary through time.

Each of these is a door to a more realistic model, and most of them are worth walking through only when the data demand it.
